title: Definite objects
intro: Until now, objects have been bare: *Kitap okuyorum* (I'm reading a book). This unit adds the accusative `-(y)I`, which marks an object as definite: *Kitabı okuyorum* (I'm reading the book). It also explains why *kitap* turns into *kitabı*, a sound change you'll meet before every suffix that starts with a vowel, and where objects go in the sentence.

sections.title: The book, not a book: the accusative

blocks.text: English shows that an object is definite with **the**. Turkish has no word for **the**; instead, a definite direct object takes the accusative (*belirtme hâli*), `-(y)I`. It follows four-way harmony, and after a vowel it takes the buffer *y* of [unit 7](gp-buffer-y-cases).

**Bare or marked?** A bare object is indefinite or general: some cheese, a newspaper, any film. An object in the accusative is a particular thing that you and your listener can both pick out: the coffee on the table, the newspaper I just mentioned.

items.note: the coffee we both know about

blocks.text: **Always in the accusative.** Names of people and places, personal pronouns, and *bu*, *şu* and *o* standing alone are definite by nature, so as objects they always take the ending. So does a noun with *bu*, *şu* or *o* in front of it.

Only direct objects take the accusative. Subjects never do, and the verbs of [unit 7](gp-dative) keep their own case: *Ayşe'ye bakıyorum* (I'm looking at Ayşe), *köpekten korkuyorum* (I'm afraid of the dog).
French marks the difference with the article, je bois du café / je bois le café; Turkish marks it with the case ending: *kahve içiyorum* / *kahveyi içiyorum*.

*Bir* and the accusative together mean **a certain** one, a particular thing you have in mind: *Bir kitabı arıyorum* (I'm looking for a particular book). For just **a book**, leave the object bare: *Bir kitap arıyorum*.

Many words that end in p, ç, t or k change that consonant when a suffix beginning with a vowel follows: p becomes b, ç becomes c, t becomes d, and k becomes ğ. This is consonant softening (*ünsüz yumuşaması*). After n, k becomes g instead of ğ.

Only suffixes that start with a vowel cause it: the accusative, the dative and, in [unit 9](gp-possessive-softening), the possessive. Before a suffix that starts with a consonant the word stays as it is: *kitapta*, *kitaptan*, *kitaplar*. That is why [unit 7](gp-dative) avoided *kitaba* and *mutfağa*.

**Words that keep their consonant.** Most one-syllable words don't soften: *süt* → *sütü* (the milk), *et* → *eti* (the meat), *top* → *topu* (the ball), *saç* → *saçı* (the hair), *park* → *parkı*. A few common ones do, and are worth learning as you meet them: *renk* → *rengi*, *kap* → *kabı* (the container), *uç* → *ucu* (the tip). Some longer loanwords keep their consonant too: *saat* → *saati*, *bilet* → *bileti* (the ticket).

items.note: a loanword that keeps its t

blocks.text: Names keep their spelling even where the sound softens: *Mehmet'i* (said *Mehmedi*), *Zonguldak'a*. Only common nouns show the change in writing.
Dictionaries show the softened form after the word: *kitap, -bı*; *çocuk, -ğu*; *süt, -tü* means it doesn't soften. When a noun ends in p, ç, t or k, check it once.

sections.title: Beni, seni, onu: pronouns as objects

blocks.text: Pronouns always point to someone definite, so as objects they always take the accusative. The forms are regular.

*O* adds the n of [unit 5](gp-pronoun-n), and so do *bu* and *şu*: *bunu* (this, this one), *şunu* (that one). The plurals add no n: *bunları*, *şunları*, *onları*. This explains *Seni seviyorum* from [unit 6](gp-present-continuous-uses): *sen* + `-I`.

The question words follow: *kim* → *kimi* (whom), *ne* → *neyi*. *Kimi bekliyorsun?* (Who are you waiting for?) With *ne*, the bare form is the usual one, *Ne istiyorsun?* (What do you want?); *neyi* asks which of several known things: *Neyi arıyorsun?* (What are you looking for?)

Some verbs take a direct object in Turkish but a preposition in English: *beklemek* (wait **for**), *aramak* (look **for**), *dinlemek* (listen **to**). So: *Seni bekliyorum*, *Seni arıyorum*, *Beni dinliyor musun?* Others go the other way: *bakmak* (look at) takes the dative, *Bana bakıyor*.

The neutral order of a Turkish sentence is subject, object, verb: *Ayşe kahve içiyor*. A bare object is glued to its verb: it comes right before it, and nothing else can come between them. *Ayşe sabah kahve içiyor* (Ayşe drinks coffee in the morning), not *Ayşe kahve sabah içiyor*.

A definite object is freer. It often comes early in the sentence, and other words can stand between it and the verb: *Kahveyi şimdi içiyorum* (I'm drinking the coffee now), *Ekmeği marketten alıyorum* (I buy the bread at the supermarket).

**Focus.** The word right before the verb carries the focus, the new or important information, as with `mI` in [unit 4](gp-question-mi). Moving a word into that slot changes what the sentence is about:

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: It's Mehmet who's buying the bread.
Mehmet buys the bread at the supermarket.

items.en: Ayşe is the one drinking the coffee.
I'm the one buying the apples.

blocks.text: Question words like *kim* and *ne* sit in that focus slot too: *Kahveyi kim içiyor?* The answer puts its new information in the same place: *Kahveyi Ayşe içiyor*.
Where you buy something takes the ablative, the place it comes **from**: *Ekmeği marketten alıyorum*. English says **at** or **from** the supermarket.

summary: A bare object means **a** or **some**: *Kahve içiyorum*. A definite object takes `-(y)I`: *Kahveyi içiyorum*.
Names, pronouns and nouns after *bu*, *şu*, *o* are always definite: *Ayşe'yi*, *seni*, *bu filmi*.
Before a vowel, final p, ç, t, k usually soften to b, c, d, ğ (g after n): *kitabı*, *ağacı*, *simidi*, *çocuğu*, *rengi*.
Most one-syllable words and names keep their consonant: *sütü*, *eti*, *Mehmet'i*.
Pronouns: *beni, seni, onu, bizi, sizi, onları*; *bunu*, *şunu*; *kimi*.
A bare object sits right before the verb; a definite one can move. The slot before the verb carries the focus: *Kahveyi Ayşe içiyor*.
